subject: English
source: National Curriculum Year 5 English (relative clauses, modal verbs, parenthesis, cohesion, poetry, suspense writing); The Eagle by Tennyson (public domain); Drive English folder held no KS2 material so content is otherwise original

lessons.title: Relative clauses
objectives: Identify relative pronouns and relative clauses
Add relative clauses to sentences with correct punctuation

keywords.def: a clause that gives extra information about a noun, starting with who, which, that, whose, where or when
a word such as who, which, that or whose that introduces a relative clause
a clause that makes sense on its own
a word naming a person, place or thing

starter: Bismillah. Underline the conjunction: I stayed in because it rained.
Write an expanded noun phrase about a library.
What is a pronoun? Give two.

teach.heading: Adding information
bullets: A relative clause adds detail about a noun
The girl who won the race is my cousin.
who, which, that, whose, where, when
teach.note: Begin with a short sentence: 'The teacher smiled.' Ask: which teacher? Add: 'The teacher who runs the reading club smiled.' Explain that who refers to a person, which to a thing, that to either.

teach.heading: Who, which and that
teach.note: Provide examples: 'The book which I borrowed was long.' 'The boy whose bag was lost cried.' Ask pupils to choose the correct pronoun. Misconception: using 'which' for people.

teach.heading: Where and when
bullets: The park where we play is large.
I remember the day when we planted the tree.
teach.note: Show how these words also begin relative clauses. Ask pupils to produce oral sentences about the school, using where and when.

teach.heading: Commas and relative clauses
bullets: My uncle, who lives in Leeds, is a doctor.
teach.note: Contrast: 'The dog that barks loudly is mine' (needed to identify the dog) and 'My dog, which is called Biscuit, barks loudly' (extra). This distinction is sophisticated; support but do not overload. Test: if you remove the clause, does the sentence still make sense?

teach.heading: Embedding clauses
bullets: The mosque stands on the hill.
The mosque, which was built in 1890, stands on the hill.
teach.note: Take a simple sentence and embed a clause in the middle. Read aloud. The examples are invented; pupils may use their own.

practice: Choose the relative pronoun: The man ___ fixed the car was kind. (who/which)
Add a relative clause: The bridge ___ was old.
Add commas: My brother who is ten loves football.
independent: Combine ten pairs of sentences using a relative pronoun.
Write six sentences about people and places using who, which, whose, where.
Edit five sentences to add the missing commas.
exit: Write a sentence with 'whose'.
Add commas: The library which is next to the mosque is quiet.
lessons.homework: Write five sentences about your family or neighbours using relative clauses.
lessons.send: SEND: give sentence halves to match. EAL: provide a table of relative pronouns with examples. Stretch: write a sentence with two relative clauses.

lessons.title: Modal verbs and adverbs of possibility
objectives: Use modal verbs to show degrees of certainty
Use adverbs of possibility such as perhaps and certainly

keywords.def: a verb such as can, could, may, might, will, would, should, must that shows possibility or obligation
how likely something is
a word like perhaps, surely, definitely, probably
being completely sure

starter: Bismillah. Add a relative pronoun: The boy ___ lost his coat cried.
Punctuate: My aunt who lives in Cairo visited us.
Write a sentence with a fronted adverbial.

teach.heading: What are modal verbs?
bullets: They show how likely or necessary something is
teach.note: Introduce modal verbs as helping verbs that go before another verb in its base form: 'might rain', 'must go'. Misconception: adding -s or -ing after a modal verb.

teach.heading: A scale of certainty
teach.note: Draw a scale on the board. Place modal verbs on it. Sentences: 'It will rain', 'It may rain', 'It might rain'. Ask pupils to change the meaning by changing the modal verb.

teach.heading: Adverbs of possibility
teach.note: Explain that these adverbs show how sure we are. Compare 'definitely' and 'perhaps'. They can go at the start or before the main verb.

teach.heading: Obligation and permission
teach.note: Link to school rules: 'You must wear uniform. You may ask for help.' Connect to adab: we should say salaam when we enter. Be careful to describe etiquette in general terms.

teach.heading: Use in writing
bullets: Predict: The storm might arrive tonight.
Warn: You must not touch the wires.
teach.note: Pupils write predictions and advice. Emphasise that modal verbs are useful when discussing possibilities in persuasive, informative and narrative writing.

practice: Put in order from most to least certain: might, will, could.
Complete: I ___ be late, so please start without me. (may/will)
Rewrite using perhaps: It may snow.
independent: Write six sentences showing different levels of certainty about tomorrow's weather.
Write a list of advice for a new pupil using should, must and may.
Rewrite four sentences replacing the modal verb to change the meaning.
exit: Which is more certain: might or will?
Write a sentence using probably.
lessons.homework: Write a short forecast for next week using modal verbs and adverbs of possibility.
lessons.send: SEND: give a certainty scale card. EAL: practise with spoken predictions. Stretch: explain why 'definitely might' sounds wrong.

lessons.title: Parenthesis: brackets, dashes and commas
objectives: Add extra information using brackets, dashes or commas
Check that a sentence still makes sense without the parenthesis

keywords.def: extra information added to a sentence
curved marks ( ) around parenthesis
long lines - used to separate extra information
a mark that can separate extra information

starter: Bismillah. Write a sentence with the modal verb might.
Add a relative clause to: The garden was beautiful.
Name three modal verbs.

teach.heading: Extra information
bullets: The sentence makes sense without it
teach.note: Write the sentence and cover the bracketed words. The sentence still works. That is the test for parenthesis.

teach.heading: Three ways to punctuate
bullets: Brackets: The shop (which opens at nine) was busy.
Dashes: The shop - which opens at nine - was busy.
Commas: The shop, which opens at nine, was busy.
teach.note: Show the same sentence three ways. Explain that brackets feel quiet, dashes feel dramatic and commas are neutral. Use a pair of marks, one before and one after.

teach.heading: Make sure you use a pair
bullets: Don't forget the comma or full stop outside
teach.note: Check pupils do not use only one dash or one comma. Model a test: remove the parenthesis and read the sentence again.

teach.heading: Where can it go?
bullets: After a noun: My uncle (a baker) arrived.
After a verb: She ran - quickly - home.
At the end: We went to the park (finally).
teach.note: Experiment with different positions. Ask which is best and why. Link to writing for effect.

teach.heading: Use in writing
bullets: Add an aside to show personality
teach.note: Show a short paragraph with three parentheses: 'The ship - an old wooden vessel - creaked.' Ask pupils to find and explain them.

practice: Add brackets: My sister aged six loves painting.
Add dashes: The lion a fierce hunter roared.
Add commas: Our teacher Mr Khan is kind.
independent: Add parenthesis to ten sentences using different punctuation.
Write six sentences about a school trip using parenthesis.
Edit sentences with missing marks.
exit: Add brackets to: The bus which was late arrived.
What test shows that something is parenthesis?
lessons.homework: Write five sentences about your family using parenthesis.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight the parenthesis first. EAL: practise with three types of mark in colour. Stretch: use parenthesis within a complex sentence.

lessons.title: Cohesion: linking ideas across sentences and paragraphs
objectives: Use adverbials to link sentences and paragraphs
Keep verb tense consistent

keywords.def: how ideas link together in a text
a word or phrase about when, such as meanwhile
shows when something happens
a group of sentences about one idea

starter: Bismillah. Add parenthesis: Hana my friend sings well.
Write a modal verb sentence.
Use a relative pronoun in a sentence.

teach.heading: Linking words
teach.note: Show a text where each sentence is separate. Add linking adverbials to show how ideas connect. Ask pupils to find the links.

teach.heading: Linking paragraphs
bullets: Start a paragraph with a link
teach.note: Explain that paragraphs signal a change of time, place, topic or speaker. Model: 'By the next morning, the storm had passed.' Ask pupils to find paragraph openers in a book.

teach.heading: Consistent tense
bullets: Stay in the past or present
Wrong: He walked in and sees a snake.
Right: He walked in and saw a snake.
teach.note: Read a sample with tense errors aloud. Ask pupils to find the verb that shifts. Misconception: switching tenses while telling a story.

teach.heading: Pronouns and cohesion
bullets: Check it is clear who 'they' are
teach.note: Revisit Year 4 learning on pronouns. Take an example paragraph and underline references. Praise clarity.

teach.heading: Edit a paragraph
teach.note: Provide a short paragraph with deliberate errors. Edit it together on the board. Pupils then edit a second paragraph independently.

practice: Add a linking adverbial: ___, we reached the village.
Correct the tense: Yesterday I go to the shop and bought bread.
Write a paragraph opener showing a change of time.
independent: Edit two paragraphs: add linking adverbials and fix tense.
Write a four-sentence account of a journey using time, place and number adverbials.
Rewrite a paragraph so that it uses a different link in each sentence.
exit: Write a linking adverbial of place.
Spot the tense error: The boy opens the door and walked in.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph about a family outing using at least four linking adverbials.
lessons.send: SEND: provide link words on cards. EAL: use time lines. Stretch: write two paragraphs with a clear link between them.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Reading The Eagle
objectives: Read a poem aloud with expression
Explain what a poem is about using evidence

keywords.def: a group of lines in a poem
a steep rough rock
bright blue
a flash of lightning with a crash of thunder

starter: Bismillah. Add a linking adverbial: ___, the sun set.
Correct the tense: She runs and fell.
Add parenthesis: The eagle a powerful bird flew.

teach.heading: Meet the poem
bullets: The Eagle by Alfred, Lord Tennyson
It describes an eagle on a cliff
teach.note: Introduce Tennyson as a famous Victorian poet. Read the poem aloud twice. He clasps the crag with crooked hands; / Close to the sun in lonely lands, / Ring'd with the azure world, he stands. / The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls; / He watches from his mountain walls, / And like a thunderbolt he falls. (Alfred, Lord Tennyson, The Eagle) Ask pupils what picture they see.

teach.heading: Understanding the words
teach.note: Use context and images. Ask how the eagle is described in the first stanza (still, high up) and in the second (hunting, falling).

teach.heading: What happens?
bullets: Stanza 1: the eagle stands high up
Stanza 2: it watches and then dives
teach.note: Ask pupils to summarise each stanza in a sentence. Highlight the change from stillness to action. Link to the final line as a dramatic climax.

teach.heading: The bird's point of view
bullets: The sea 'crawls' from the eagle's height
We see the world as the eagle does
teach.note: Ask: how does the sea look from a mountain? Why does it 'crawl'? Link to perspective. Be cautious: ask for pupils' ideas first.

teach.heading: Respond to the poem
bullets: What does the poem make you feel?
teach.note: Invite personal responses. Link to appreciating the beauty of creation. Mention that the Qur'an invites reflection on birds: Surah al-Mulk 67:19 refers to birds above us with wings spread and folded. Keep it brief and respectful.

practice: What does 'azure' mean?
In which line does the eagle attack?
How many lines are in each stanza?
independent: Read the poem aloud with a partner, one stanza each.
Answer six questions about the poem.
Draw the scene and label with words from the poem.
exit: Which word shows the eagle is strong?
What does the final line suggest?
lessons.homework: Learn the first stanza by heart.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight key words and use picture support. EAL: pre-teach crag, azure, thunderbolt. Stretch: write a short paragraph on how the poem's mood changes.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Figurative language: simile, metaphor, personification
objectives: Identify simile, metaphor and personification
Explain the effect of figurative language in the poem

keywords.def: a comparison using like or as
saying one thing is another
giving human actions to non-human things
what a word or phrase makes the reader think or feel

starter: Bismillah. Recite the first stanza of The Eagle.
What is a stanza?
Add parenthesis: The eagle a huge bird flew.

teach.heading: Simile
teach.note: Ask what makes the comparison powerful: speed and force. Ask pupils to create their own simile for a falling eagle.

teach.heading: Metaphor
bullets: He clasps the crag with crooked hands
teach.note: Note that 'hands' is used metaphorically for the eagle's talons. Explain that metaphor is stronger than simile because it is direct. Ask pupils for examples from everyday use.

teach.heading: Personification
bullets: The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls
teach.note: Show how the sea is given the ability to crawl. Ask what this suggests: slow, low, small. Contrast with the eagle's power.

teach.heading: Explain the effect
bullets: Say what it makes us imagine
teach.note: Model: 'Tennyson uses personification when he says the sea "crawls". This makes the sea seem slow and small from the eagle's height.' Pupils write one more.

teach.heading: Use figurative language
teach.note: Pupils create a simile, metaphor and personification about a storm. Share and improve. Check each is correctly labelled.

practice: Is this a simile or a metaphor: The moon is a silver coin.
Name the technique: The wind howled in anger.
Make a simile for a fast runner.
independent: Find and label three examples of figurative language in The Eagle.
Explain the effect of two examples.
Write a simile, a metaphor and an example of personification about the sea.
exit: Name the technique: The sun smiled down.
Write one simile about an eagle.
lessons.homework: Collect five examples of figurative language from books or poems and label them.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards for technique and example. EAL: use pictures to explain comparisons. Stretch: write a paragraph comparing two figurative phrases.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Sound and structure: rhyme, alliteration and rhythm
objectives: Identify rhyme scheme, alliteration and rhythm
Perform a poem with expression

keywords.def: words that end with the same sound
words close together that begin with the same sound
the beat of the words in a poem
the pattern of rhymes in a poem

starter: Bismillah. Name the three types of figurative language.
Is 'the sea crawls' a simile or personification?
Write a metaphor about a mountain.

teach.heading: Rhyme
bullets: Each stanza has one rhyme sound
teach.note: Tap out rhymes while rereading. The rhyme scheme is AAA BBB. Ask why a triplet (three rhyming lines) might help give a feeling of power.

teach.heading: Alliteration
bullets: clasps the crag with crooked hands
teach.note: Underline the 'c' sounds in the first line and the 'w' sounds in the second stanza. Ask what the hard 'c' sounds suggest, such as grip and strength.

teach.heading: Rhythm
bullets: Count the beats in each line
The lines have a strong steady beat
teach.note: Clap the rhythm. Note that each line has four strong beats. Do not over-explain. Pupils feel the pattern. Ask whether the last line sounds quicker.

teach.heading: Perform it
bullets: Pause at semicolons and full stops
teach.note: Model a performance. Show how punctuation guides the voice. Pairs rehearse and perform. Offer feedback on clarity and expression.

teach.heading: Why sounds matter
teach.note: Draw out the idea that poets choose words for sound as well as meaning. Contrast hard sounds (c, k, t) with soft sounds (s, l, m) and invite pupils to give their own examples.

practice: Which word rhymes with 'lands'?
Find two words in the poem that begin with the same sound.
How many lines are in the poem?
independent: Label the rhyme scheme and alliteration in the poem.
Perform the poem with a partner and record two improvements.
Write four lines using alliteration about a river.
exit: Write two alliterative words for a storm.
What is the rhyme scheme of The Eagle?
lessons.homework: Write a four-line rhyming verse about a bird.
lessons.send: SEND: use coloured pens to mark rhyme and alliteration. EAL: practise reading in chunks. Stretch: write a short analysis of how sound supports meaning in the final line.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Writing our own nature poem
objectives: Plan and write a short poem about an animal
Use figurative language and sound devices deliberately

keywords.def: a section of a poem
words that create pictures in the mind
first version
improve

starter: Bismillah. Name two sound devices.
Write a simile about a hawk.
What is personification?

teach.heading: Choose your subject
bullets: Choose one you can picture clearly
teach.note: Brainstorm animals and what they do. Link to the beauty of creation: observing creatures is a way to reflect on Allah's creation. Avoid attributing statements to texts that are not certain.

teach.heading: Gather words
teach.note: Model gathering vocabulary for 'The Owl' or 'The Fox'. Encourage precise verbs. Ask pupils to find unusual but accurate words.

teach.heading: A model poem
bullets: The fox slips through the silver frost,
a shadow stitched to the sleeping hedge.
teach.note: Read the model. Identify alliteration (slips... silver... sleeping), personification, metaphor ('Moonlight is his lantern'). Ask what picture the poem creates. Show how the poem uses two short stanzas.

teach.heading: Write a draft
bullets: Aim for a strong last line
teach.note: Pupils write drafts. Circulate to suggest improved verbs. Reassure pupils that their poems need not rhyme.

teach.heading: Reading and improving
bullets: Change one word to make it stronger
teach.note: Pairs share and give a star and suggestion. Ask volunteers to perform. Celebrate effort.

practice: Write three precise verbs for your animal.
Write one metaphor.
Write one phrase with alliteration.
independent: Write a poem of two stanzas about an animal.
Label the figurative language in your poem.
Write a title.
exit: Which line is your best?
What sound device did you use?
lessons.homework: Improve your poem and write a neat copy.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a word bank and frame. EAL: allow a draft in simple sentences first. Stretch: write in rhyme with a consistent scheme.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Suspense - reading and writing a tense scene
lessons.title: Reading a suspense extract
objectives: Identify how an author builds suspense
Infer feelings from details in a text

keywords.def: a feeling of excitement or worry about what will happen
nervous strain in a story
three dots ... showing a pause or something unfinished
the mood of a setting

starter: Bismillah. Recall: name three poetry devices.
Add parenthesis: The house an old one stood still.
Write a linking adverbial for the start of a paragraph.

teach.heading: What is suspense?
bullets: The reader wants to know what happens next
The pace slows or speeds up
teach.note: Ask pupils about moments in films or books where they felt tense. Explain that suspense is created by what the author chooses to show and hide.

teach.heading: Read the extract
bullets: Light shines from a door that should be dark
teach.note: The old house was silent. Nadia crept up the stairs, her hand sliding along the cold banister. One step creaked. She froze. Somewhere above her, something shifted. A long, slow scrape ... then nothing. Her heart hammered. The door at the top of the stairs was open - just a crack - and a thin line of yellow light spilled onto the landing. She had not left a light on. Had she? Read slowly in a hushed voice.

teach.heading: Techniques
teach.note: Underline each technique. Ask pupils what each does. Short sentences increase pace; an ellipsis creates a pause; the question leaves the reader uncertain.

teach.heading: What do we infer?
teach.note: Ask how we know. Use evidence: 'Her heart hammered', 'She had not left a light on'. Model a P.E.E. answer.

teach.heading: What happens next?
teach.note: Link to modal verbs. Pupils predict: 'Nadia might find a stranger, or perhaps a cat.' Ask them to justify with clues.

practice: Find a short sentence that shows Nadia was afraid.
What does 'Her heart hammered' suggest?
What is unusual about the light?
independent: Answer six questions about the extract with evidence.
Create a table: technique, example, effect.
Write a prediction using modal verbs.
exit: Name one way the author builds suspense.
Write one inference about Nadia.
lessons.homework: Find a tense moment in a book you are reading and note the techniques.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight techniques in colour. EAL: pre-teach banister, landing, froze. Stretch: write a short paragraph on how the pace changes.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Suspense - reading and writing a tense scene
lessons.title: Suspense techniques in writing
objectives: Use short sentences, senses and questions to create tension
Vary sentence length for effect

keywords.def: how fast or slow a story moves
a sentence with few words that creates drama
describe actions and details instead of naming feelings
a question that does not need an answer

starter: Bismillah. What is suspense?
Give one technique used in the extract.
Add an ellipsis to this: Then nothing happened.

teach.heading: Show, don't tell
bullets: Show: Her hands shook. She held her breath.
Details make readers feel the fear
teach.note: Offer a flat sentence and ask pupils to show the feeling instead. Collect actions for fear: trembling, frozen, wide eyes, pounding heart.

teach.heading: Control the pace
teach.note: Show a paragraph with a mix: a long sentence full of detail followed by a very short one. Ask what the short sentence does. Warn against overuse of short sentences.

teach.heading: Use the senses
teach.note: Pupils add sensory detail to a plain sentence about a dark room. Check for accuracy and avoid clichés.

teach.heading: Questions and ellipsis
teach.note: Explain that a question can pull the reader into the character's thinking. Ellipsis shows pause. Show overuse as an error: too many questions and dots weaken the tension.

teach.heading: Build a paragraph
teach.note: Model an opening for 'The Cellar'. Write three sentences together and mark techniques. Pupils create their own opening.

practice: Rewrite to show, not tell: He was nervous.
Write a short sentence to make the reader jump.
Add a sound to: The cellar was dark.
independent: Write a suspense paragraph of six sentences using at least three techniques.
Label the techniques you used.
Improve two sentences by showing feelings.
exit: Write one rhetorical question for a tense scene.
Why do we vary sentence length?
lessons.homework: Write four sentences showing fear without using the word 'scared'.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and a sense word bank. EAL: act out feelings. Stretch: write using the second person for suspense.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Suspense - reading and writing a tense scene
lessons.title: Planning and writing a suspense scene
objectives: Plan a short suspense scene with a beginning, build-up and cliffhanger
Draft using the techniques learnt

keywords.def: an ending that leaves the reader wanting more
where and when the story happens
an outline of what will happen
a group of sentences about one idea

starter: Bismillah. Write a short sentence for tension.
Show the feeling: She was worried.
Add a linking adverbial: ___, the door creaked.

teach.heading: Choose a scene
teach.note: Offer choices and let pupils choose. Discuss what makes each location tense. Remind pupils that the scene should be safe, but exciting.

teach.heading: Plan in four steps
bullets: 2. A small sign of something wrong
teach.note: Model a plan for 'The Attic'. Step one: Layla goes up to fetch a box. Step two: a small noise. Step three: she sees movement. Step four: a hand on the box ... Pupils plan their scene.

teach.heading: Plan your language
teach.note: Ask pupils to jot the language they plan to use in the margin of the plan. Collect examples on the board.

teach.heading: Write the opening
teach.note: Model the opening: 'At the top of the narrow stairs, the attic door stood half open.' Pupils write theirs. Circulate and support.

teach.heading: Write on
teach.note: Remind pupils to reread and fix tense. Allow time to write. Share one strong line from each group.

practice: Write your setting in one sentence.
Write a short sentence for step two.
Write a cliffhanger final line.
independent: Complete a four-step plan.
Write the first two paragraphs of your suspense scene.
Underline three techniques in your draft.
exit: Which technique have you used most?
What is your cliffhanger?
lessons.homework: Finish your suspense scene (paragraphs three and four).
lessons.send: SEND: use a writing frame. EAL: rehearse sentences orally. Stretch: add a parenthesis and a relative clause.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Suspense - reading and writing a tense scene
lessons.title: Editing and improving our suspense writing
objectives: Edit work using the grammar and punctuation learnt this half term
Spell words ending in -able and -ible

keywords.def: check carefully for errors
improve writing
a common word ending, as in comfortable
a word ending, as in possible

starter: Bismillah. Spell: possible, comfortable, sensible.
Add commas: My cousin who lives in York is visiting.
Correct the tense: She opened the door and sees a shadow.

teach.heading: Editing checklist
teach.note: Display the checklist. Model checking a paragraph. Ask pupils to tick each item and fix mistakes using a purple pen.

teach.heading: Spelling -able and -ible
bullets: -able usually follows a full word: comfort-able
-ible often follows a root that is not a word: poss-ible
teach.note: Explain the general pattern. Mention that there are exceptions and that we learn the common words. Dictionary use is encouraged.

teach.heading: Improve vocabulary
bullets: Check each word earns its place
teach.note: Show weak verbs (went, said) and strengthen them. Use a thesaurus carefully. Check the new word fits.

teach.heading: Peer feedback
bullets: Say what created the most tension
teach.note: Model respectful feedback. Link to adab of advising each other kindly. Pupils write one improvement.

teach.heading: Publish
bullets: Read it aloud to the class
teach.note: Invite volunteers to read. Praise effective techniques. Reflect on progress this half term.

practice: Spell: visible, terrible.
Correct: The door opens slowly and a shadow moved.
Add parenthesis: The attic a dusty room was silent.
independent: Edit your suspense scene with the checklist.
Improve five sentences with better vocabulary.
Write a neat final copy of your first paragraph.
exit: Name one change you made.
Spell a word ending in -ible.
lessons.homework: Practise reading your scene aloud with suitable pace.
lessons.send: SEND: use a shortened checklist. EAL: focus on spelling and verb tense. Stretch: rewrite the cliffhanger in two different ways.
